title: 10 Dishes That Explain Valencia
description: From rice cooked over orange wood to eel stew beside the Albufera, these dishes trace Valencia through its huerta, lagoon, seafront, market counters and midmorning table.

cards.title: Paella valenciana — Casa Carmela
cards.subtitle: Malvarrosa’s wood-fired rice tradition
cards.notes: The restaurant requires advance ordering for paella valenciana and prepares only a limited number each day.
cards.short_summary: Casa Carmela cooks its paella valenciana over orange wood with chicken, rabbit, local beans and other ingredients from the surrounding land. It shows how Valencia’s defining rice dish is inseparable from the huerta and the controlled, communal rhythm of cooking one pan for a table.

cards.title: Clóchinas al vapor — Casa Montaña
cards.subtitle: Valencia’s small, seasonal Mediterranean mussel
cards.notes: Clóchinas are seasonal; availability follows the local harvest rather than a year-round menu cycle.
cards.short_summary: Visit València identifies Casa Montaña as a place serving clóchinas in their classic steamed form. Cooked largely in their own juices with restrained seasoning, they put seasonality and the city’s working waterfront directly on the table.
cards.source_title: Da comienzo la temporada de las clóchinas, ¡a disfrutarlas! — Visit València

cards.title: Arroz al horno — La Riuà
cards.subtitle: Rice leaves the paella pan for the oven
cards.notes: The current menu lists arroz al horno with raisins and chickpeas.
cards.short_summary: La Riuà’s arroz al horno broadens the city’s rice vocabulary beyond paella. Its oven-baked preparation and combination of rice, chickpeas and raisins reveal a cuisine comfortable with casseroles, concentrated stock and pantry ingredients as well as open-fire spectacle.

cards.title: Horchata con fartons — Horchatería Daniel
cards.subtitle: Chufa becomes a drink, pastry becomes a utensil
cards.notes: Daniel’s official shop sells horchata and fartons together; the venue also operates inside Valencia’s Mercat de Colón.
cards.short_summary: The pairing explains Valencia in one practical gesture: dip the long, soft farton into chilled horchata made from local chufa. Daniel treats the two as a single order, reflecting how the drink and pastry function together rather than as separate curiosities.
cards.source_title: Horchata y fartons artesanos — Horchatería Daniel

cards.title: Bunyols d’abadejo — Central Bar
cards.subtitle: Salt cod fritters at the Mercado Central counter
cards.notes: The direct menu offers the fritters by the plate or individually.
cards.short_summary: Central Bar’s bunyols d’abadejo turn preserved cod into a compact market snack. Their place on a counter menu inside Mercado Central captures Valencia’s ease with eating in motion while shopping, and with transforming salted fish through batter and frying.
cards.source_title: Plats — Central Bar by Ricard Camarena

cards.title: Coca d’oli con titaina y anguila ahumada — Bodega Anyora
cards.subtitle: Cabanyal flavors carried on a thin savory coca
cards.notes: Listed on Anyora’s weekday set menu; dishes on this menu can change.
cards.short_summary: Anyora layers titaina and smoked eel onto coca d’oli. Tomato-and-pepper relish, fish and flatbread bring together three durable strands of Cabanyal cooking: garden produce, preserved seafood and dough built to carry a meal.

cards.title: All i pebre — Restaurant L’Illa
cards.subtitle: Eel and potatoes beside the Albufera
cards.notes: The restaurant identifies all i pebre as a house specialty and names eel and potatoes as its base.
cards.short_summary: At L’Illa in El Palmar, all i pebre keeps the Albufera’s eel at the center of the plate, supported by potatoes and a garlic-and-paprika sauce. It explains the lagoon as a food landscape, not merely scenery south of the city.

cards.title: Esgarraet valenciano — Enboga-Bar
cards.subtitle: Roasted vegetables meet salt cod
cards.notes: Enboga’s version combines cod, roasted pepper, aubergine and hard-boiled egg.
cards.short_summary: Enboga’s esgarraet sets sweet roasted pepper and aubergine against salted cod, then adds egg. The dish explains a recurring Valencian pattern: produce from the land given definition by preserved fish and enough oil and juice to demand bread.
cards.source_title: Carta de arroces, fideuàs y mariscos — Enboga-Bar València

cards.title: Fideuà de gamba, cigala y rape — Enboga-Bar
cards.subtitle: The paella pan, recast with toasted noodles
cards.notes: The menu requires a minimum order for two people and specifies number-four noodles, prawn, langoustine and fish.
cards.short_summary: Enboga’s fideuà replaces rice with toasted noodles while retaining the broad, iron-pan method and a concentrated rock-fish stock. It shows how Valencia’s neighboring coastal traditions share equipment and social form even when the principal starch changes.
cards.source_title: Carta de arroces, fideuàs y mariscos — Enboga-Bar València

cards.title: Figatell with mushrooms and onion jus — Bodega Anyora
cards.subtitle: A butcher’s preparation in a modern neighborhood menu
cards.notes: Anyora’s weekday menu names the dish as “El Figatell de Eladio” with shiitakes, onion jus and mashed potato; availability may change.
cards.short_summary: Anyora serves figatell—a compact preparation traditionally built around pork and liver—with mushrooms, onion jus and potato. It adds inland butchery and whole-animal cooking to a Valencian story too often reduced to rice and seafood.
